newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African ethnic group wins official recognition.
newsitem.headline: S.African ethnic group wins official recognition.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela's government has officially added a new category to South Africa's complex ethnic mix, despite having opposed the racial classifications of apartheid.

Mpho Mosimane, spokesman for Constitutional Development Minister Mohammed Valli Moosa, said in an interview on Wednesday the Griquas had won official recognition as a separate ethnic community on Tuesday.
"It is a breakthrough for the Griquas in the sense that there is now official recognition," Mosimane said.
"In terms of history, the Griquas were completely destroyed, more even than the Zulus, Tswanas, all those groups...They were more trampled upon than any other community," he said.

The Griquas trace their roots to the second half of the 18th century when Dutch and other European settlers began moving into the interior from the Cape colony and had children with indigenous Bushmen and Hottentot (Khoisan) inhabitants.
Under South Africa's previous apartheid system of racial classification, the Griquas were lumped with the Coloureds, being anyone of mixed white-black descent.
A central tenet of apartheid was that all South Africans should be classified by race or tribe and forced to live as far as possible in separate territories.
Mandela's government, mainly as a sop to white Afrikaners, has said that while apartheid in any form was unacceptable, it was willing to guarantee the cultural and linguistic rights of minorities.
The Griquas themselves, living in scattered communities mainly in the Northern Cape province, always objected to being classified as Coloureds and demanded recognition as the heirs of the Bushmen.
Few racially pure Bushmen remain in South Africa. They were persecuted both by the white settlers and by black tribes moving down from the north.

"It was a historical moment. For the first time the government accepts that they are a community," Mosimane said, adding that recognition would give the Griquas greater clout in national policy making.
"For them, that is very important...They will no longer be approaching the government as individuals," he said.
Mosimane said the government would not intervene in the Griqua community's long-standing internal leadership feud.
Two main groups claim to represent the community, the Griqua People's Organisation and the Griqua National Conference.
In October the Griqua People's Organisation wrote a letter to Britain's Queen Elizabeth demanding compensation for land which British colonialists confiscated from them in the last century.
The group also claimed rights to diamond-rich land near Kimberley now owned by De Beers Consolidated Mines.
No reliable figure is available for the number of Griquas, but some estimates put the maximum at about 20,000.
